lead: This unit follows the shear flow in the walls of a thin-walled aircraft beam: where it runs under a shear force, where the shear centre sits, and how a closed box, a multi-cell wing or an open stringer carries torque. After it you can work out the shear flow in open, closed and mixed sections, locate the shear centre, solve single- and multi-cell boxes, idealise a wing into booms and panels, correct for taper, and size a buckled web by Wagner's theory.
about: The first chapter defines shear flow and the shear centre on a channel. The open-section chapter integrates from a free edge, on a Z-section and on a channel stiffened by booms. The closed-section chapter cuts the loop and adds a constant flow, and shows how a thick front wall moves the shear centre forward. Bredt–Batho torsion follows for one cell, then the multi-cell chapter adds equal twist and solves a six-boom two-cell box under lift with a short program. Idealisation, taper and mixed open-and-closed sections come next, then the tension field of a buckled web, and the unit closes with the weak torsion of open sections against a closed box made from the same strip.

chapters.idea: Shear flow q is the shear force carried per unit length of wall, in N/mm; the shear centre is the point in the cross-section through which a transverse load must act so the beam bends without twisting.
chapters.depth: q = τ·t where τ is the shear stress in the wall (N/mm²) and t its thickness (mm). Show that the shear flow in a wall varies along the wall and that its resultant is a single force; the line of that resultant is the shear centre. Cover: free edge as the point where q = 0, resultant by integrating q round the section, shear centre of doubly symmetric sections (at the centroid), singly symmetric sections (on the axis of symmetry, offset along it), channel and lipped-channel positions. Some syllabi call the shear centre the flexural centre or the centre of twist. Keep the arithmetic of a full shear flow distribution for 5.2.
chapters.figure: blocks: free edge → q(s) built up → resultant force → offset e to the shear centre
chapters.example: A channel section has a web 120 mm deep, flanges 60 mm wide, uniform thickness 3 mm, and carries a vertical shear force S = 5 kN. Find the shear flow at the flange–web junction when the load acts through the centroid, and the distance e of the shear centre from the web centre line.
chapters.trap: Treating the centroid as the shear centre. In a channel the two are far apart, and the twist this causes is what the chapter is about.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 (second moments of area, unsymmetrical bending) and Unit 1 (wing structure).
chapters.leave: The full closed-section algebra goes to 5.3; the torsion formulas go to 5.4 and 5.10.

chapters.idea: In an open thin-walled section the shear flow at any point is the integral of the direct stress gradient from a free edge, so the whole distribution follows from the shear force and the section second moments.
chapters.depth: Derive q from equilibrium of a small wall element: for bending about the x axis, q = −(S/I<sub>xx</sub>)∫ t·y·ds, where S is the shear force (N), I<sub>xx</sub> the second moment (mm⁴), t the thickness (mm), y the distance from the centroidal axis (mm) and s the distance along the wall from the free edge (mm). State the unsymmetrical form using I<sub>xy</sub> without long derivation. Cover: shear flow distributions in I, C, Z and lipped sections; sign reversal of q; resultant and shear centre of an unsymmetrical open section by taking moments of q about a convenient point; boom-idealized stringer sections.
chapters.figure: plot: q against distance s round a Z-section, positive on one flange, negative on the other, with the resultant shown passing through the shear centre
chapters.example: A Z-section has flanges 40 mm wide and a web 80 mm deep, all 2 mm thick, and carries S = 3 kN parallel to the web. Compute the shear flow at 10 mm intervals round the section, sketch the distribution, and find the shear centre position.
chapters.trap: Getting the sign of the integral wrong, and forgetting that q is zero only at the free edge — not at every flange tip you happen to pick.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for the definition of q and the shear centre; Unit 4 for I<sub>xx</sub> and I<sub>xy</sub>.
chapters.leave: Closed loops to 5.3; tapered beams to 5.7.

chapters.idea: Cut the closed loop at one point to make it an open section, compute the basic shear flow q<sub>b</sub>, then add a constant q₀ round the loop chosen so the section twists by the correct amount.
chapters.depth: For a shear load acting through the shear centre the correct amount of twist is zero, so q₀ is found from ∮(q/t)ds = 0 taken round the mean line. Cover: choice of the cut, which is imaginary and can be anywhere; the resulting q = q<sub>b</sub> + q₀; shear flow distribution and shear centre of symmetrical and unsymmetrical closed sections; the extra check that the applied shear equals the resultant of q. Work in numbers throughout; typical wall thickness 1–3 mm and box sizes 100–400 mm.
chapters.figure: blocks: make an imaginary cut → compute q<sub>b</sub> as an open section → add constant q₀ → set twist to zero → shear centre offset
chapters.example: A rectangular box is 200 mm wide and 100 mm deep with a uniform 2 mm skin, and carries a vertical shear force S = 10 kN through the mid-point of the vertical wall. Find q<sub>b</sub> at the corners, the value of q₀, and the distance the shear centre lies from the wall.
chapters.trap: Forgetting q₀ altogether, or picking the cut at a corner and then assuming q there is zero in the real closed section.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for q<sub>b</sub>; 5.4 for the zero-twist condition written in Bredt form.
chapters.leave: Torque-carrying closed sections to 5.4 and 5.5; multi-cell compatibility to 5.5.

chapters.idea: A closed thin-walled tube carries torque by a constant shear flow round its wall, and both the stress and the twist rate depend only on the enclosed area and the perimeter.
chapters.depth: Bredt-Batho results: q = T/(2A), τ = q/t = T/(2At), and rate of twist dθ/dz = (T/(4A²G))∮(ds/t), with T the torque (N·mm), A the area enclosed by the mean line (mm²), t the wall thickness (mm), G the shear modulus (N/mm²) and s measured along the mean line (mm). Equivalent torsion constant J = 4A²/∮(ds/t). Derive q by taking moments of the wall shear about any point inside the loop. State the assumptions: thin wall, closed loop, constant q round the loop, free warping, no buckling. Some syllabi call this Bredt's formula. Compare with the solid circular shaft result τ = T·r/J for sanity.
chapters.figure: blocks: torque T → constant shear flow q = T/(2A) → wall stress τ = q/t → twist rate from ∮(ds/t)
chapters.example: An elliptical wing box has a mean-line area A = 0.25 m², mean perimeter 1.8 m, skin thickness 2 mm and G = 27 GPa. It carries a torque T = 40 kN·m. Find the shear flow, the shear stress in the skin, and the twist per metre of span.
chapters.trap: Using the outer contour area instead of the area enclosed by the mean line, and using Bredt for a section that is not closed.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for q; Unit 2 for the twist–torque relation of a shaft.
chapters.leave: Many cells to 5.5; open walls to 5.10; warping restraint to later study.

chapters.idea: A multi-cell box shares torque between cells that all twist at the same rate, so the unknowns q₁, q₂, … are fixed by one torque equation plus one equal-twist equation per pair of cells.
chapters.depth: Torque share T = Σ 2A<sub>i</sub>q<sub>i</sub>, plus equal twist rate (1/(2A<sub>i</sub>G))∮(q/t)ds for each cell, giving a small linear system — two cells means two equations in two unknowns. Cover: two- and three-cell boxes; a wall shared by two cells carries the difference q<sub>i</sub> − q<sub>j</sub>; walls effective and ineffective in bending (a wall that cannot take direct stress still takes shear); the same linear system for a shear load, with the equal-twist condition used to find the shear centre. Some syllabi ask for this to be solved as a matrix in MATLAB; the method is the same, only the solver changes. Include a wing-box and a fuselage example.
chapters.figure: blocks: applied torque → split into q₁ and q₂ → equal twist per cell → solve two equations → shear flow in every wall
chapters.example: A two-cell box has cell areas A₁ = 40 000 mm² and A₂ = 25 000 mm². The outer walls are 1.5 mm thick, the common wall 2 mm, G is constant, and the torque is 20 kN·m. Find q₁, q₂ and the shear flow in the common wall.
chapters.trap: Adding q₁ and q₂ in the shared wall instead of subtracting them, and dropping the equal-twist condition.
chapters.prereq: 5.4 for one cell; 5.3 for the shear-load version.
chapters.leave: Combined open-plus-closed sections to 5.8; buckled webs to 5.9.

chapters.idea: A real wing section is replaced by a few booms that carry all the direct stress and thin panels that carry only shear, which turns a hard integral into a short sum.
chapters.depth: Boom area B = A<sub>stringer</sub> + (t·b/6)(2 + σ<sub>skin</sub>/σ<sub>boom</sub>), where A<sub>stringer</sub> is the stringer area (mm²), t the skin thickness (mm), b the stringer pitch (mm) and the stress ratio accounts for the skin working at a different stress from the stringer. Cover: choosing booms and panels; idealized section properties I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub> from boom areas and positions; shear flow in the panels of an idealized section, q = −(S/I<sub>xx</sub>)Σ B·y for booms cut off by the panel; direct stress in a boom σ = M·y/I<sub>xx</sub>. Names: boom idealization, lumped area method, stringer–skin idealization.
chapters.figure: blocks: real wing section → stringers plus skin → effective boom areas → idealized section → I and panel shear flows
chapters.example: A rectangular wing box is 400 mm wide and 200 mm deep with four corner booms of area 150 mm² and a 2 mm skin. Find the effective boom areas, I<sub>xx</sub>, and the panel shear flows for a vertical shear force S = 15 kN.
chapters.trap: Counting the skin twice: its effective width belongs to the boom, while the panel still carries shear. Also using the wrong factor for a corner boom shared by two panels.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for the shear flow sum; Unit 4 for direct stress in bending.
chapters.leave: Bending stresses in the real, unidealized section stay in Unit 4; tapered cases go to 5.7.

chapters.idea: In a tapered beam the boom load changes along the span, and the spanwise component of that changing load adds a taper shear flow on top of the ordinary bending shear flow.
chapters.depth: Boom load P = M·y/I<sub>xx</sub> (N); along a taper the boom axis is inclined, so a boom force has a component along the beam. The extra shear flow at a cut equals minus the sum of the spanwise rates of change of the boom loads cut off by that panel: q<sub>taper</sub> = −Σ (dP/dz). Total q = q<sub>bending</sub> + q<sub>taper</sub>. Cover: a tapered spar with two booms; a swept tapered wing box; how taper shifts the shear centre; wing and fuselage shear flow distributions. Keep the taper angles small so the small-angle approximations hold.
chapters.figure: blocks: bending moment gradient → boom load P → boom slope dy/dz → taper shear flow added to panel q
chapters.example: A spar is idealized as two booms 200 mm apart, each of area 250 mm². The boom spacing tapers linearly from 200 mm at the root to 120 mm over a 2 m span, and the root bending moment is 40 kN·m. Find the taper shear flow in the web at the root and compare it with the bending shear flow there.
chapters.trap: Using only the local bending moment and ignoring the taper term, and getting the sign of dP/dz wrong.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 and 5.6 for the boom model, Unit 4 for M and I<sub>xx</sub>.
chapters.leave: Buckled webs to 5.9; a full wing aeroelastic solution to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Real sections mix closed cells with open flanges, so each cell is cut and the constant q₀ values are found from compatibility between the cells and the open part.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Method: cut every closed cell, compute q<sub>b</sub> as if the whole section were open from the cuts, then impose zero twist on each cell and equality of twist where cells share a wall. Cover one closed cell with an attached open flange carrying a shear load, and the torque case with an open boom taking direct stress. Keep to two unknowns.
chapters.figure: blocks: cut each cell → basic q<sub>b</sub> on the open skeleton → unknown q₀ per cell → compatibility → final shear flow
chapters.example: A section has one rectangular cell 150 mm × 80 mm with 2 mm walls and an open flange 60 mm long and 2 mm thick attached at one corner. It carries a vertical shear force of 6 kN. Find the shear flow in the cell walls and in the open flange.
chapters.trap: Treating the whole section as closed and applying Bredt straight away, or ignoring the direct stress carried by the open flange.
chapters.prereq: 5.3 for closed sections, 5.2 for open parts, 5.5 for the compatibility idea.
chapters.leave: Buckled webs to 5.9; fatigue and failure of these sections to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A thin web that has buckled in shear still carries load as a diagonal tension field, and Wagner's theory gives the shear flow and the boom loads for that field.
chapters.depth: When the web shear stress reaches the buckling stress the web wrinkles along one diagonal and the load travels as a tension band inclined at angle α to the flanges. Wagner's theory introduces a diagonal tension factor between 0 (pure beam shear, web unstressed after buckling) and 1 (fully developed tension field); the web shear stress is limited by the buckling stress and the rest of the shear is carried by the flanges as axial load. Cover: web buckling in shear (cross-reference Unit 6), the diagonal tension band, the split of applied shear between web and booms, boom axial loads, and the beam that is called a Wagner beam or a thin-webbed beam with diagonal tension. Some syllabi call this tension field theory.
chapters.figure: blocks: applied shear → web buckles → diagonal tension band at angle α → boom axial loads plus web shear
chapters.example: A thin-webbed beam has a web 500 mm deep and 1.5 mm thick, boom area 300 mm² each side, and carries a shear force of 80 kN. Using Wagner's theory, estimate the diagonal tension angle, the share of the shear carried by the web, and the resulting axial load in each boom.
chapters.trap: Applying ordinary beam shear stress τ = S/(t·d) to a buckled web: after buckling the web stress cannot keep rising with the load.
chapters.prereq: 5.6 for the boom–panel model; Unit 6 for shear buckling of plates.
chapters.leave: Actual plate buckling coefficients stay in Unit 6; post-buckling of stiffened panels also stays there.

chapters.idea: An open thin wall resists torque only through St Venant torsion, with torsional stiffness proportional to the cube of the wall thickness, so it is orders of magnitude weaker than the same material formed into a closed box.
chapters.depth: For a thin-walled open section, J = (1/3)Σ b·t³, where b is the wall length (mm) and t its thickness (mm); τ<sub>max</sub> = T·t<sub>max</sub>/J and twist θ = T·L/(G·J) over length L. The shear stress varies linearly across the wall thickness, zero at the mid-thickness and maximum at the surfaces. Cover: properties of an angle, tee or Z stiffener; comparison of an open wall with the equivalent closed box of the same material and perimeter, which shows the factor of 100–1000 in stiffness; warping of the open section. Mention restrained (non-uniform) torsion only in one line, as beyond this unit. This is why aircraft boxes are closed.
chapters.figure: plot: shear stress across the wall thickness of an open section, zero at mid-thickness and maximum at both surfaces
chapters.example: A 60 mm × 60 mm × 2 mm equal angle, 2 m long, with G = 27 GPa, carries T = 200 N·m. Find J, the maximum shear stress and the total twist. Then form the same 240 mm of material into a closed 60 mm × 60 mm box with a 2 mm wall and compare the twist for the same torque.
chapters.trap: Using the Bredt formula on an open section, which overstates J by a large factor, and measuring b at the outer face instead of along the wall centre line.
chapters.prereq: 5.4 for the closed-box comparison; Unit 4 for the twist–torque relation.
chapters.leave: Warping restraint and non-uniform torsion beyond one line; stiffener design to Unit 6.
